Yet by 2023, after a century in which they grew under three different systems, Latvia stood at \pctwc{2023} per cent of the Western core, Estonia at \pctx{Estonia}{Western}{2023} and Lithuania at \pctx{Lithuania}{Western}{2023}: the region as a whole had moved from \pctx{Baltics}{Western}{1913} to \pctx{Baltics}{Western}{2023} per cent, a gain of eighteen percentage points over 110 years, and against the Nordic countries Latvia had fallen from \pctnord{1913} to \pctnord{2023} per cent. The Western periphery, the group of poorer Western economies to which the Baltic states belonged by income in 1938, rose over the same century from \pctx{Periphery}{Western}{1913} to \pctx{Periphery}{Western}{2023} per cent. Within the region the ranking reversed: Latvia, the richest Baltic economy in 1913, in 1938 and in all but a handful of years to 1988 (Estonia stood marginally above it in the aftermath of each war, 1919--23 and 1947--8, and in 1962--4), is now the poorest, and Lithuania, the poorest for most of the century, is the richest. The sections below take the three regimes in turn. \subsection{Interwar capitalism, 1913--1940} The First World War and the collapse of the empires gave Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia their first opportunity to build independent states, and left them in ruins. The German advance of 1915 stabilised along the Daugava, within reach of Riga, for two and a half years; the imperial government evacuated Latvia's industry eastwards, and most of it never returned; Riga lost more than half its population between 1914 and 1919 \parencites[107]{ehbaltics_tarvel}[616]{norkusmark2021}[103]{karnups_2017_neatkarigas}. Table~\ref{tab:war} places the result beside the other belligerents. Between 1913 and 1919 Latvia lost 35 per cent of its population, 59 per cent of its GDP and 37 per cent of its income per head, Lithuania 36, 60 and 38 per cent; of the European economies for which estimates exist, only the Soviet Union lost as large a share of its output. Estonia, untouched by major fighting until 1918, lost less. Pre-war Latvia had been called the `Belgium of the East' for its industry and living standards; by 1919 it resembled Belgium in the devastation it had suffered relative to its size \parencite[77]{hiden_salmon}. \input{../../Tables/latvia/T10_war.tex} The 1920s were a decade of reconstruction rather than growth. Lithuania regained its 1913 income per head by 1923, Estonia by 1925, Latvia only in \lvREGAINthirteen{}: the recovery was most protracted where the pre-war economy had been most integrated into the Russian market and most of the industrial capacity had been lost \parencites[95--6]{aldcroftthirdworld}[103]{eastern_crampton}[6]{norkus_2025_denmarkisation}. Between 1913 and 1929 income per head in the three countries together was unchanged (Table~\ref{tab:growth}), while the Western core grew by \grx{Western}{1913}{1929} per cent a year and Czechoslovakia, Berend's `success story of the twenties', by 45 per cent \parencite[243]{Berenddecadesofcrisis}; Latvia's 1922--9 growth of \gr{1922}{1929} per cent a year was bounce-back growth from a very low base, financed by foreign capital, and it stopped when the pre-war level was regained. The new states rebuilt on the land. Agrarian reforms expropriated the estates of the Baltic-German and Polish nobility, which had held between a quarter and a half of all land, and created a class of smallholders; gold-backed currencies were introduced in 1922 (Latvia and Lithuania) and 1928 (Estonia); exports were redirected from Russia to Britain and Germany and shifted from manufactures to butter, bacon, flax and timber, in conscious imitation of Denmark \parencites[115]{baltichistorykasekamp2017}{norkus_2025_denmarkisation}[121]{vaskela_1996_land}. Agriculture still employed 67 per cent of the Latvian labour force in the late 1930s and 63 and 74 per cent of the Estonian and Lithuanian (Table~\ref{tab:structure}). The 1930s look different. Between 1929 and 1938 income per head grew by \gr{1929}{1938} per cent a year in Latvia, \grx{Lithuania}{1929}{1938} in Lithuania and \grx{Estonia}{1929}{1938} in Estonia, against \grx{Western}{1929}{1938} per cent in the Western core, \grx{Periphery}{1929}{1938} in the Western periphery and \grx{ECE}{1929}{1938} in East-Central Europe; among European economies only the Soviet Union, whose figures for the period are contested, and Finland grew as fast, and all three Baltic states closed their gap with the Western core by six to ten percentage points (Table~\ref{tab:relative}).\footnote{Rosés and Wolf's Maddison-based estimates give Latvia 4.1 per cent a year over 1929--38 against 4.9 for the Soviet Union, and the authors note that the Latvian and Estonian figures may be on the high side \parencite[188, 190]{roseswolf2010}.} The Depression was shallower and shorter than in most of Europe: Lithuania avoided recession altogether, and Latvia's and Estonia's downturns of 1931--3, of 10 and 8 per cent from peak to trough, resembled those of the Nordic countries, which are regarded as among the mildest on the continent, although Latvia's banking crisis of 1931, in which three joint-stock banks failed, was more severe \parencites{grytten_nordicdepression}[91]{bernankegd01}[236]{terleckaspinigai}. The Baltic performance has usually been read, by contemporaries and by Aldcroft, as the fruit of export-led agricultural modernisation \parencites[189]{balticstates1938}[119--20]{aldcrof1914}. The sectoral evidence does not support that reading. Trade openness fell sharply after 1929, in Latvia from 38 to 22 per cent of GDP,\footnote{Period averages of 1925--9 and 1935--8 (Table~\ref{tab:structure}); the single-year ratios of Norkus and his co-authors, built on the same GDP series, fall from 49 per cent in 1929 to 27 in 1938 \parencite[10]{norkus_2025_why}.} the processed share of exports fell in both Latvia and Estonia, and the Baltic states remained the most agrarian and least industrial part of Europe outside the Balkans (Table~\ref{tab:structure}). What grew was industry for the home market: Latvian industrial output rose by \sgr{Industry}{1929}{1938} per cent a year over 1929--38, a rate exceeded among capitalist economies only by Lithuania and matched only by Finland, behind import-substituting tariffs, state enterprises and the infant-industry policies that the authoritarian governments of the 1930s, Lithuania's dating from 1926 and Estonia's and Latvia's from 1934, adopted as part of their `economic nationalism' \parencites[116]{ehbaltics_tarvel}{karnups_2017_karla}{Klimantas2024}. Latvia was the one Baltic economy in which the shares of both agriculture and industry in GDP rose in the 1930s at the expense of services, the result of heavily subsidised agriculture and the pruning of the public administration \parencites[683]{latvija19141945vesture}[135--6]{karnups_2017_karla}. The growth of the 1930s was achieved not through international trade but despite its contraction \parencite[188]{valge_1994_tartu}. \input{../../Tables/latvia/T9_structure.tex} The verdict on the interwar regime is mixed. Over 1913--38 as a whole, Latvian and Estonian income per head grew marginally faster than the Western core's, by \gr{1913}{1938} and \grx{Estonia}{1913}{1938} against \grx{Western}{1913}{1938} per cent a year, and Lithuanian marginally slower; the region's position relative to the core, \pctx{Baltics}{Western}{1913} per cent in 1913 and \pctx{Baltics}{Western}{1938} in 1938, did not change. The 1930s were among the most dynamic years the region has known, and by 1938 Latvia and Estonia retained the places among the best-performing peripheral economies of Europe that they had held in 1913, which is what Aldcroft meant in calling the Baltic states the most promising of Europe's backward regions \parencite[105, 171]{aldcroftthirdworld}. But the interwar years also disposed of a belief that has shaped Baltic self-perception ever since: that Latvia and Estonia stood level with Finland. They had been close in 1913, Latvia at \pctfin{1913} per cent of the Finnish level; by 1938 Latvia stood at \pctfin{1938} per cent and Estonia at \pctx{Estonia}{Finland}{1938}, because Finland grew at \grx{Finland}{1913}{1938} per cent a year through the two decades while the Baltic economies spent the first of them recovering what the war had destroyed. The difference was not primarily one of social capability: Latvian literacy, though below Finnish (11 per cent of Latvians aged ten and over were illiterate in 1935, under 1 per cent of Finns aged fifteen and over in 1930), was high for the European periphery, and Latvian university enrolment per head, 4.3 per thousand in the 1930s, was nearly double the Western core's and, in Kalniņš's contemporary comparison, the highest in the Baltic \parencites{klimantas2025thesis}[102--3]{norkusdvides}. It was one of resources and markets. Finland's forests gave it an export staple for which Western demand recovered quickly after 1920 and which carried an engineering sector with it; the Baltic states had lost the only large market their industry had ever served, and the food exports that replaced it faced Danish competition and British quotas. \subsection{Soviet socialism, 1940--1991} The Soviet occupation of June 1940, the German occupation of 1941--4 and the renewed fighting of 1944 cost Latvia and Estonia a fifth or more of their population, Lithuania within its actual borders a twentieth, and the three, on the present estimates, between 28 and 48 per cent of their income per head (Table~\ref{tab:war}). The losses were demographic before they were material: deportations, the Holocaust, war deaths and the flight of some 250,000 people to the West in 1944 removed more than a million people, among them a disproportionate share of the professional and commercial classes; the fall in income per head, 28 per cent in Latvia and 29 in Estonia, was correspondingly smaller than the fall in output, and roughly half the per-capita losses that Table~\ref{tab:war} records for Austria, the Netherlands or Poland. Lithuania's larger fall is examined in the companion paper. Recovery was rapid, as it was everywhere in the Soviet sphere: Latvia regained its 1938 level of total GDP in \sregain{GDP}, Estonia its 1939 level in 1948 and Lithuania in 1949, and with smaller populations their income per head regained the 1938 level in 1946, \lvREGAINthirtyeight{} and 1948 respectively, two years before the Western core or periphery regained theirs. The war had destroyed people rather than plant; with a fifth of the population of the northern republics gone, capacity stood underused, and the early recovery rested on putting labour, increasingly immigrant labour directed from Russia, back to work on existing capital, the mechanism that Vonyó and Markevich identify across post-war East-Central Europe \parencites[290]{vonyoinmorys2021}[108]{years_of_dependence}. The command economy was installed within five years. Industry and banks were nationalised in 1940--1 and again in 1945--7; the republics were incorporated into the all-Union planning system in 1946; and the deportations of 1948--53, which removed some 42,000 people from Latvia, 100,000 from Lithuania and 35,000 from Estonia, the largest single operation being that of March 1949, which took more than 40,000 people from Latvia and some 30,000 and 21,000 from Lithuania and Estonia, broke the resistance of the countryside to collectivisation, which was essentially complete within two years (Table~\ref{tab:collectivisation}) \parencites[183]{krumins_2017_tautsaimnieciba_1940}[99--100]{feest2014}[102--3]{years_of_dependence}.
